why: Promote. (1) There were zero 5xx and zero non-200 responses across all 9785 requests, on both the canary (2411) and stable (7374). (2) Per-endpoint p95 is at parity: the worst canary-vs-stable p95 gap across /browse, /search and /checkout is 1 ms (<=2 ms). (3) The behaviour is stable over the whole test: in all four 30 s windows the canary p95 is within 5 ms of stable (worst delta 4 ms, in the final 90-120 s window) and no window has any 5xx, so there is no drift or late-test degradation. (4) The only asymmetry in the dashboard is canary /browse p99 77 ms vs stable 28 ms, but both versions share the identical 87 ms maximum and the canary simply has a slightly higher rate of slow requests (13/1200 = 1.08% vs 15/3672 = 0.41%), with no canary request exceeding the stable ceiling. Judgement: that p99 gap is small-sample tail noise from a single pod taking ~25% of traffic hitting the same pre-existing slow path, not a new failure mode introduced by 1.1; with no errors, p95 parity per endpoint and across time, and no new latency ceiling, the release-blocking cost of a rollback is not justified. Judgement: recommend promoting while watching /browse p99 and 5xx rate during ramp-up, since 462 canary /checkout requests is a thin sample for rare-event risk.

claims.claim: Across all 9785 requests there were zero 5xx responses and zero non-200 responses on both versions (canary 2411 requests, stable 7374).
Per-endpoint p95 latency is at parity: the largest canary-vs-stable p95 gap across /browse, /search and /checkout is 1 ms.
In every 30 s window of the 120 s test the canary p95 is within 5 ms of stable (worst delta 4 ms) and no window contains any 5xx.

The canary's higher /browse p99 sits under the same 87 ms maximum as stable and reflects only a higher slow-request rate (13/1200 = 1.08% of canary requests over 50 ms vs 15/3672 = 0.41% on stable), with no canary request above the stable ceiling.
